title: Ethereum protocol milestone candidates
selectionPolicy: Frontier genesis is an origin marker. Visible knots are limited to events that materially changed Ethereum's operating phase, consensus, fee market, scaling model, staking lifecycle, or broadly useful execution behavior; routine, preparatory, difficulty-only, parameter-only, and future upgrades are excluded.

candidates.summary: Frontier was Ethereum's first live mainnet release, producing genesis block 0. It was deliberately bare-bones and aimed at technical users, but established the programmable mainnet represented by this chronology.
candidates.inclusionReason: It is the conceptual and chronological origin of the artifact; use a pith/genesis marker so it is not confused with later protocol knots.
candidates.disputes: ethereum.org identifies genesis as block 0, while EIP-6953 lists Frontier's upgrade activation trigger as block 1. This dataset uses block 0 for genesis and does not treat block 1 as a second event.

candidates.summary: Homestead was Ethereum's second major release and moved the network beyond the deliberately bare-bones Frontier phase. It introduced several protocol changes, DELEGATECALL, and devp2p forward-compatibility rules that supported later upgrades.
candidates.inclusionReason: It marks Ethereum's first major operational maturation after launch and is historically recognizable.
candidates.disputes: The announcement predicted an approximate Pi Day time; the exact timestamp is the observed value in ethereum.org's chronology.

candidates.summary: The DAO fork applied an irregular state change that moved affected DAO balances into a recovery contract. Some participants rejected the intervention and continued the unforked chain, now Ethereum Classic.
candidates.inclusionReason: It is an exceptional protocol intervention with lasting chain-governance significance; its exploit remains a separate scar event.
candidates.disputes: This record is the protocol fork, not the earlier DAO smart-contract exploit. Do not describe the exploit as an Ethereum protocol hack or merge its loss amount into this milestone.

candidates.summary: Byzantium was the first Metropolis-stage fork. It expanded EVM error handling and cryptographic capabilities, delayed the difficulty bomb, and reduced the block reward from 5 ETH to 3 ETH.
candidates.inclusionReason: Its broad EVM, cryptographic, receipt, and issuance changes make it the defining 2017 protocol upgrade.
candidates.disputes: Metropolis is the parent development phase, not an alias for a single activation; Byzantium and Constantinople remain separate events.

candidates.summary: Constantinople and St. Petersburg activated together at the same block. Constantinople added CREATE2 and other EVM improvements while St. Petersburg simultaneously removed EIP-1283 after the originally planned activation was postponed for a security concern.
candidates.inclusionReason: The simultaneous pair completed the Metropolis phase and introduced enduring execution features; one knot avoids inventing two events at one block.
candidates.disputes: The upgrade has two canonical names because two protocol changes occurred at block 7,280,000. Use Constantinople as a compact label only if the detail view retains St. Petersburg.

candidates.summary: The Beacon Chain began producing proof-of-stake blocks after its minimum deposit conditions were met. It initially ran beside proof-of-work mainnet without executing user transactions, then became Ethereum's consensus layer at The Merge.
candidates.inclusionReason: It is the independent launch of the consensus system that now secures Ethereum and begins the proof-of-stake chapter before The Merge.
candidates.disputes: The configured MIN_GENESIS_TIME was 12:00:00 UTC; ethereum.org records the produced genesis block at 12:00:23 UTC. The deprecated contemporary alias Eth2 should not be the primary display name.

candidates.summary: London redesigned Ethereum's transaction fee market. EIP-1559 introduced a dynamically adjusted base fee that is burned and a separate priority fee, alongside several other EIPs in the fork.
candidates.inclusionReason: It is Ethereum's most recognizable fee-market change and materially altered transaction pricing and ETH supply mechanics.
candidates.disputes: London contained five EIPs, so EIP-1559 is its headline feature rather than a complete synonym for every fork change.

candidates.summary: The Merge ended proof-of-work block production on Ethereum mainnet and adopted the Beacon Chain's proof-of-stake consensus. Ethereum retained its execution state and complete transaction history through the transition.
candidates.inclusionReason: This is the largest consensus change in Ethereum history and the chronology's most important single protocol knot.
candidates.disputes: The activation trigger was terminal total difficulty, not a scheduled block. PoW block 15,537,393 crossed the threshold and block 15,537,394 was the first post-Merge block; Bellatrix nine days earlier was preparatory and is excluded.

candidates.summary: Shanghai execution changes and Capella consensus changes activated synchronously. Together they enabled partial and full validator withdrawals from the Beacon Chain to the execution layer.
candidates.inclusionReason: It completed the initial proof-of-stake lifecycle by making staked principal and rewards withdrawable.
candidates.disputes: Shapella is the conventional combined short name; Shanghai and Capella are the execution- and consensus-layer names respectively.

candidates.summary: Dencun introduced ephemeral blob transactions and a separate blob fee market through EIP-4844. This gave rollups a cheaper data-availability path than transaction calldata and laid the foundation for later data-availability sampling.
candidates.inclusionReason: Blob transactions changed Ethereum's scaling architecture and are central to the rollup-oriented roadmap.
candidates.disputes: The EF announcement rounds the time to 13:55 UTC; the maintained chronology records 13:55:35. Dencun is the combined short name for Cancun and Deneb.

candidates.summary: Pectra introduced EIP-7702 EOA code delegation and major validator-management improvements. These included higher effective balances, execution-triggered exits, on-chain deposit processing, and increased blob capacity.
candidates.inclusionReason: It delivered broadly legible account and staking changes while advancing scaling, making it more than a routine bundle.
candidates.disputes: Pectra is the combined short name for Prague and Electra; there is no material date dispute.

candidates.summary: Fusaka's headline PeerDAS change distributed blob custody and sampling across nodes instead of requiring every node to download every blob. It enabled safer blob-throughput scaling and also added execution-layer resource limits and repricing.
candidates.inclusionReason: PeerDAS is a structural change to Ethereum's data-availability model and the latest activated named upgrade before the cutoff.
candidates.disputes: Official sources use both Fulu–Osaka and Osaka/Fulu ordering; Fusaka is the stable combined label. The later BPO forks are separate parameter-only exclusions.

exclusions.summary: Frontier Thawing lifted the restrictive launch gas limit and enabled ordinary transactions. It was an important stabilization step, but its story is subordinate to genesis and Homestead.
exclusions.exclusionReason: Avoids over-marking Ethereum's first months while retaining the more legible genesis and maturation events.

exclusions.summary: Tangerine Whistle and Spurious Dragon were emergency responses to 2016 denial-of-service attacks, repricing underpriced operations and clearing state. They materially protected network health but would add two more knots to an already dense 2016 ring.
exclusions.exclusionReason: Preserve visual spacing and reserve headline knots for Homestead and the exceptional DAO protocol intervention.
exclusions.disputes: This grouped exclusion contains two distinct activations; it must not be converted into one dated production event.

exclusions.summary: Istanbul repriced EVM operations, improved DoS resilience, reduced cryptography and calldata costs, and added CHAINID. Its changes were meaningful, but less distinct in a sparse public chronology than the same-year Constantinople/St. Petersburg milestone.
exclusions.exclusionReason: Maintains a small visible set and avoids two general-purpose execution upgrades in 2019.

exclusions.summary: Muir, Arrow, and Gray Glacier each postponed Ethereum's proof-of-work difficulty bomb. They maintained usability while proof of stake was prepared, but their narrative function is subsumed by The Merge.
exclusions.exclusionReason: They are single-purpose maintenance forks and would dilute the major-transition vocabulary.
exclusions.disputes: This grouped exclusion contains three distinct activations and must not become one production event.

exclusions.summary: Berlin repriced state access and introduced typed transaction envelopes and optional access lists. These are durable execution improvements, but London five months later provides a more distinct fee-market narrative.
exclusions.exclusionReason: One 2021 knot is sufficient for the sparse view, and London has higher recognizability and narrative value.

exclusions.summary: Altair was the first Beacon Chain upgrade and added sync committees; Bellatrix prepared consensus clients for The Merge. Both are technically important, but their narrative is already bounded by Beacon Chain genesis and The Merge.
exclusions.exclusionReason: Avoids turning preparation for the consensus transition into multiple adjacent knots.
exclusions.disputes: This grouped exclusion contains two distinct activations and must not become one production event.

exclusions.summary: BPO1 and BPO2 were preconfigured parameter-only forks that raised blob targets and maxima after Fusaka. They changed capacity without introducing a new named protocol feature set.
exclusions.exclusionReason: Parameter tuning should not share the same visual prominence as a named structural upgrade; Fusaka already represents the enabling change.
exclusions.disputes: BPOs are real fork activations but intentionally excluded from the named-milestone vocabulary.

exclusions.summary: Glamsterdam is the next named Ethereum upgrade and was planned for Q4 2026 as of the research cutoff. Its highlighted work includes enshrined proposer-builder separation and block-level access lists, but no mainnet activation date or epoch had been announced.
exclusions.exclusionReason: It falls after the 2026-08-21 cutoff and has not activated; future roadmap points must not appear as completed knots.
exclusions.disputes: Feature scope and timing remain subject to change until an official mainnet announcement. Re-evaluate only after activation.

exclusions.summary: Hegotá is roadmap work intended to follow Glamsterdam, with later upgrades even further out. These future items are unactivated, incompletely scoped, and outside the research cutoff.
exclusions.exclusionReason: Future roadmap planning is not historical protocol chronology and is subject to change.
exclusions.disputes: Naming and scope may change before activation.
